Title: Tram Lines: Going Slow Is What Gets Your Wheels Caught
Description: The beginner's instinct at a tram rail is to slow down, and that is the move that puts a wheel in the gap. A certified coach's first method is a narrow scissor stance with most of your weight — about eighty percent — on the back foot, and speed kept up. Speed is your best friend here: a slow wheel has time to find the rail. Filmed with a street skater in Amsterdam. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Cross a Tram Rail Square On, Never at a Slant
Description: How to cross tram rails on skates: a wheel drops into the gap when it meets it along its length. The fix is geometry: step over the tracks in a wide pizza angle, the V position opened up, so that each wheel crosses the gap perpendicular to it. A certified coach calls these pizza steps and puts them in the beginner's first three methods. It looks clumsy and it works. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: Tram Lines: Push From a T When There Is No Room to Build Speed
Description: How to push off when a tram line leaves no room to build speed. A certified coach's answer for the tight spots is a T stance: one skate set across behind the other, planted between the tracks, so you can push off and keep your momentum where there is no space to build any. Same idea as the scooting push, aimed at a gap. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: The Small Jump Over a Rail Is All About the Landing
Description: A certified coach files the small jump under intermediate and says the work is in the landing: absorb it with a deep knee-over-toe bend, stay low without ever straightening your legs, and keep a slight scissor on touchdown. I would add: a jump is a choice, unlike a hill, so do not jump much at the start — and when you do, knees like springs, no panic — Cass. From ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: Crossing a Rail on One Skate: Sink Into the Strap, Do Not Hop
Description: How to cross a tram line on one skate, when the reflex is to unweight or hop the skate across the gap. A certified coach says the opposite: do not lift, sink deeper into your ankle strap for stability and let the wheel roll through. The backwards version follows the same rule — cross the gaps in a reverse scissor with your weight held securely over the trailing leg, never floating. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Title: Your Back Foot Taps Through the Turn Because Your Weight Sits on the Heel
Description: Why your back skate taps through a parallel turn to your weaker side, and how to stop it. The cause: the back knee is not bent far enough over the toes, weight sits on the heel, and that skate's front wheels unweight and skip while you force the turn. The fix: bend the back knee forward until the kneecap covers the toes, squeezing into the ankle strap. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: parallel turn inline skating, weak side turning skates, skitching back foot, turning on rollerblades

Title: Your Weak Leg Refuses to Bend, and That Is Normal
Description: The second cause of a tapping back foot: the weaker leg simply will not bend while rolling — completely normal, says a certified coach, because your body is not used to carrying its weight on that foot alone. The fix is not a turn at all. Practise a straight-line scissor stance on your weaker side, holding a deep knee-over-toe bend, before you ask that leg to turn anything. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
Keywords: weaker leg skating, scissor stance drill, non dominant side inline skating, knee bend rollerblading

Title: Turn Wide and Gentle Before You Ever Turn Tight
Description: The third cause of a skidding back foot is ambition: a sharp, tight turn attempted before the edge and the knee bend exist. The body panics and flicks the back skate round to finish the arc. A certified coach's progression is patient — wide, gentle ninety-degree curves first, and the arc tightens only as the knee bend and the balance improve, never ahead of them. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Forward Crossovers: Hold Two Seconds on One Skate First
Description: What to master before a forward crossover: gliding on a single skate for at least two seconds, says a certified coach. That is what lets you regroup after the cross without hurrying, without clipping the other skate, and without ending up stuck with both feet crossed — the worst place a skater can be. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.

Title: Hips Pushed Back Show Up as Tense, Scrunched Feet
Description: Sticking your bottom out behind you feels safe and costs you twice: a certified coach names it among the three beginner faults — it creates lower back strain and scrunched-up, tense feet. The correction: shoulders stacked over the hips, shins bent forward until the kneecaps cover the toes, weight on the front half of the feet, toes relaxed rather than gripping. Technique from ICP-certified coach Asha Kirkby. Illustration generated with AI.
